760: I talk for eight hours to people I cannot see. I assume they are enjoying it. I certainly am.
761: My job is to fill every silence with my voice. The silence never fights back, so I always win.
762: I have said good morning to more strangers than anyone alive. None of them said it back.
763: They pay me to talk. My family finds this funny. They have been asking me to stop for years.
764: I read the weather, the time, and my own opinions. Only two of those are part of the job.
765: I sit alone in a small room and speak to thousands. It is the loneliest crowd you can imagine.
766: I once talked for an hour with no notes at all. Nobody stopped me. Nobody ever stops me.
767: My voice goes out to the whole city. My voice also does not know when to be quiet. I am working on it.
768: I introduce every song like it is the greatest one ever made. I have said that about all of them.
769: The rule is do not stop talking. I have followed this rule since I was very small. Ask my parents.
770: I hear my own voice all day and I have grown quite fond of it. This may be a warning sign.
771: A listener called to say I talk too much. I put them on air so I could respond at great length.
772: I say the time out loud every few minutes. It keeps me company. The clock does not talk back.
773: My whole job is being heard and never seen. I could be wearing anything right now. I am.
774: I welcome each new hour like an old friend. There are twenty-four of them. I greet them all.
775: Children write to ask if I ever stop talking. The honest answer is only to breathe, and barely.
776: I describe the whole world to people who cannot see me. Half of them are asleep. I describe it to them anyway.
777: I said one wrong word this morning and thought about it all day. The other ten thousand were fine.
778: I greet an entire city at once, out loud. The city continues about its business without comment.
779: A tiny light turns red and suddenly I must be interesting. It has been red for eleven years.
780: I run the whole show and stand where nobody can see me. This is exactly how I like it. Mostly.
781: The actors take their bows and their flowers. I take the quiet pride of a curtain that fell exactly on time.
782: I whisper into a little headset and an entire world moves. Then it stops when I say stop.
783: Nobody claps for me. Nobody knows my name. If I vanished, though, the lights would go out at once.
784: I stand in the dark all evening making sure the light finds everyone but me. That is the job.
785: The curtain goes up because I said so. It comes down because I said so. In between, I barely breathe.
786: I keep a list of everything that must happen and when. The list is longer than the show itself.
787: Actors forget their words and look at me. I mouth the words. I am the least seen helper alive.
788: My whole night is spent making sure nothing goes wrong. When nothing does, no one notices. Perfect.
789: I have watched this show two hundred times from the exact same dark corner. I could run it asleep.
790: I press a button and it snows. I press another and it stops. I am quietly in charge of the weather.
791: The star bows and the crowd roars. I am already three steps ahead, setting up tomorrow's roar.
792: I know every secret of this building. The trapdoors, the ropes, the one squeaky board. All mine.
793: Everyone out front thinks the magic happens on its own. It happens because I am pushing buttons very fast in the dark.
794: I tell grown actors when to walk and when to wait. They listen. It is the only place they ever do.
795: My office is a dark corner with one small light. It is not glamorous. It runs the entire evening.
796: When the show ends, I am the last one out. I lock the door on a room that just held a thousand people and now holds one.
797: A child asked who is in charge back here. I said me, very quietly, and then went back to work.
798: I hold the whole show in my head, cue by cue. If I sneeze at the wrong moment, chaos. So I do not.
799: The audience never learns my name, which is fine. If they did, something would have gone very wrong that night.
